Q: VS 2022 Power Platform Tools Sign-in error 'The authentication type must be specified.' A:

I had the same issue. I found posts suggesting to clear the plugin cache, but I didn't have the plugin. Finally figured out it looks like the same files have moved to a new folder with the Power Platform tools. I cleared the files from this folder and was able to connect without issue:

C:\Users\<UserName>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\CRMDeveloperToolKit

Q: Why isn't std::initializer_list being deduced as an argument for a concept that it matches? A:

The expression {9, 255, 86, 4, 89, 6, 1, 422, 5, 29} is not implicitly a std::initializer_list.

Its meaning and its type is intended to be contextually inferred from its usage.

  • If you pass it to a function that expects a std::initializer_list<int>, then that's what it is.

  • If you pass it to a function that expects a std::array<int,10>, then that's what it is.

  • If you pass it to a function that expects an aggregate type, then that's what it is.

You, however, are passing it as a deduced template argument template <Iterable C> auto findmax(C const &c)

findmax({9, 255, 86, 4, 89, 6, 1, 422, 5, 29}) won't compile because the function relies on the call site to specify what type is being passed, and your call site is depending on the function to specify what type is being passed.

std::initializer_list isn't mentioned at either location, so the compiler does not know that you want std::initializer_list.

Q: shutil.move doesn't delete source files A:

I am doing a remarkably similar thing to you, moving photos and sorting them by year and month. Also using PIL to get the date, etc. I was also having the same problem you were having with the files not being removed in the source by the shutil.move(). I assume you saw the Windows Error saying that operation couldn't be completed because the file was being used somewhere else.

PermissionError: [WinError 32] The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process:

It seems this error is being thrown during the removal operation of shutil.move, which is why it copies successfully, but then doesn't remove. After some reading, I realized that PIL Image opens the photo, but never closes it, which is what is causing the error. So a simple rawMetadata.close() right after you assign "datetime" variable will close the file and correct the error. Then shutil.move can successful remove the file from the source directory. I did this in my code and it worked like a charm.

Q: How to use distinct inside CONCAT_WS() in MySQL? A:

A bit of a late answer, but for other people Googling try:

SELECT id, name, 
    CONCAT_WS("/",
        NULLIF(code1,""),
        CASE WHEN code2 NOT IN ('', code1) THEN code2 END, 
        CASE WHEN code3 NOT IN ('', code1, code2) THEN code3 END
    ) AS concat_code
FROM table1

The CASE is functioning as a NULLIF with multiple string values, some being the previous values to prevent duplicates.

I left out the GROUP BY id since id seems to be the primary key, that makes that statement useless.

Q: Stopping a process with Powershell A:

To add to Panagiotis Kanavos's helpful answer:

For interactive (UI-based) display and filtering of object-based PowerShell command results using PowerShell commands rather than fzf:

  • Use the built-in, GUI-based Out-GridView cmdlet, if you're on Windows and

    • either: stuck on Windows PowerShell (the legacy, ships-with-Windows, in-maintenance-only-mode Windows-only edition of PowerShell whose latest and final version is 5.1)

    • or: you're using PowerShell (Core) 7, but cannot or don't want to install supporting modules.

      • Note: While Out-GridView is a fully supported, non-deprecated part of PowerShell 7, future development in this area of functionality will focus on the install-on-demand Microsoft.Powershell.ConsoleGuiTools module and its Out-GridConsoleView cmdlet: see next point.

  • Use the install-on-demand, console (terminal)-based, PowerShell (Core) 7-only Out-GridConsoleView for cross-platform compatibility or if you prefer a terminal-based UI,[1] as well as for potential future enhancements, though as of this writing it is the built-in, Windows-only Out-GridView that offers more features.[2]

    • That is, Out-GridView, due to being based on the Windows-only WPF GUI framework, is only available in PowerShell 7 on Windows.
      By contrast, the terminal-based Out-GridConsoleView works both on Windows and supported Unix-like platforms.

    • You can install the Microsoft.Powershell.ConsoleGuiTools module that contains Out-GridConsoleView with Install-PSResource; e.g., for the current user:

      Install-PSResource -Scope CurrentUser Microsoft.Powershell.ConsoleGuiTools

Applied to the case at hand, user314159 has provided a helpful Out-GridView example in a comment on the question, which is therefore Windows only:

Poor man's one-liner for a searchable GUI to kill processes:
Get-Process | Out-GridView -OutputMode Multiple | Stop-Process -WhatIf
Note the Filter input box at the top of the form, and the -WhatIf test mode: remove the -WhatIf to actually stop the selected processes; with it, PS will only pretend to stop them.

To allow selection of (at most) only one input object, use -OutputMode Single (or -PassThru, though note that the latter doesn't work in Out-ConsoleGridView anymore; another notable difference is that Out-GridView defaults to -OutputMode None, whereas Out-ConsoleGridView defaults to -OutputMode Multiple).

[1] However, note that, like Out-GridView, Out-ConsoleGridView too, despite being a TUI (terminal/text-based user interface), does not work via PowerShell remoting.

[2] As of v0.7.7 of the module that Out-ConsoleGridView comes with, Out-GridView - only - notably offers the ability the ability to sort by a single column (click on the header of the column of interest), to hide columns (right-click on any header), and to specify multiple, column-specific filter criteria (click the icon with the down arrow next to the filter textbox).
Note that even though the module's documentation claims that at least sorting is also supported in Out-ConsoleGridView, that appears not (yet?) to be the case.
Conversely, though, the module comes with an additional cmdlet that has no built-in counterpart: Show-ObjectTree, which visualizes the input objects' properties in an expandable tree structure (albeit without the ability to select and pass objects through).

Q: Is it portable to cast an unsigned value to its signed version to prevent underflow? A:

If you do signed or unsigned math, in both cases the same hardware is used. And it will cause the same under and overflows. But in C/C++ you can not query the processors flags, so if you want to know a overflow happens you need more code to evaluate it.

Apart from that, common CPUs use the two's complement

But essentially the mapping between signed and unsigned is well-defined and both can be converted back and forth:

To better understand over and underflow, it's useful to use a number circle visualisazion:

The only difference is, a unsigned number only under/overflows at one position in the circle, signed numbers at another. Whenever your code crosses on of the borders (Min / Max) it will set the under/overflow flags in the HW (if signed is suported - which almost is the case) and essentially under/overflow by definition. You can also say, normally your HW is unsigned at most, any support for signed is just to allow more effective code. In a high level language you can just do signed math, even when the HW is pure unsigned... As it's just a different interpretation of the same binary pattterns.
